review_text_raw:
The game has a great concept and some thrilling moments. The developers did a fantastic job immersing you in the feeling of being a "cog in a machine". The music, interface design, story theme, and execution were excellent. I especially enjoyed the quiet moments where I could read through various documents and explore the backstory and world the developers created.

That’s why it pains me so much that all this hard work feels utterly underutilized. You’re essentially handheld and dragged through a linear story, with little to no impact from your choices. There are intricate mechanics that seem fun once you struggle through their first use, but they are never used again. It is just a little bit more "game" than a "interactive movie".

I don’t want to be cruel—I can see the developers put a lot of effort into it—but it was just far too short.

Cons:

* The bomb defusal mission is just nonsensical. While it's obviously designed and written to be deliberately confusing to challenge the player, it is also ridiculous. The supervisor, Skinner, would be handling this, or at least offering assistance, not just casually leaving another agent's life up to a 3rd day employee who is reading the bomb defusal manual for the first time. Was having a good time in the game up until this mission. If you look at this achievement as well, only some ~50% of players have this achievement, and then you have to wonder, of those 50% how many had to look up a walk-through online in order to complete it? 
* Game was definitely somewhat dry at times where I felt a little bit bored. 
* I won't spoil any specifics but I will say the ending of the game is...not good, in my opinion.

* Gameplay is straight forward and easy to understand. 
* Solid voice acting. 
* Storytelling is pretty engaging. 
* Game very stable, zero crashes or bugs / glitches. 
* No additional DRM beyond Steam.
* No Epic Online Services.

review_text_raw:
The Operator is a very short (3 to 4 hours at best) interactive visual novel with good production value. The interface looks clean and easy to use, the voice acting is good, and the interactive elements are pretty decent. For a visual novel. 

It is presented, however, as a game of deduction and puzzle solving. The puzzles and deductions are shallow with too much handholding. As you progress new mechanics are introduced, and then discarded immediately after. This gives the mistaken impression that much more content is waiting for you and puzzles will get more difficult. And then the game is over.

The story is equally shallow. The opening scene reveals too much, making the big reveal at the end something you can piece together within a few minutes of playing the game. The ending is a cliffhanger of sorts, but it makes this game feel like the opening chapter of a larger story that has not been written. Worse is that none of the conspiracy is ever explained, leaving you with many questions that are unlikely to be answered. There are no divergent paths, only one ending, and zero replay value.

If you go into this game expecting a visual novel, you will have an entertaining few hours with an okay story and underwhelming finale. If you go into this game expecting deduction, investigation, and puzzle solving, you will find only disappointment. This ultimately leads to my negative review. For a visual novel it is too short with an unresolved story, and for an investigation game the puzzles are too simple. The Operator has a lot of unmet potential, which is a shame.

review_text_raw:
This game has so much going on that I would ideally like to praise but a lot of those same things are also why I didn't really enjoy it.  On the bright side it has a very clever user interface system I like where most of the game is controlled via a "computer", the puzzles range from really easy to more complicated, and the story has some creativity going on.  It's definitely somewhat interesting, very dialogue heavy, and I would not recommend if you're not a strong reader, lover of puzzle games, or if you like a lot of scenery or environment changes.

With that said, the user interface becomes tiring to interact with very quickly.  It's hard to convey a sense of importance or immediate action when most of the puzzles really come down to clicking and having a computer "analyze" random clues.  The puzzles don't scale well in difficulty nor do they feel like they have a good payoff - any skill you learn will either be used again and again because we have to have some way to drive the game or it's a one time use - why did we bother to spend so much time reworking the wheel for no reason? (Example slight spoiler: you will never need to analyze anything other than the one sample in the game).  The instructions are lacking a lot - they have a help button that is definitely useful but there's an element of figure it out here that at times seems un-necessary.  I really don't understand not sticking to more tried and true puzzle formats particularly because they would have felt more rewarding, helped the game, and surely been easier to execute with more precision.

The story is the last complaint I'm going to throw out there.  It's interesting and I want to be invested, however, it is rushed, let down by a lot of bad music and sound interaction, and I found myself uninvested in the characters including my own character frequently.  Any story is going to ask you to slightly engage in disbelief but if you're an analytical or practical thinker there is going to come a point where you realize this is almost like a bad tv fiction.  If you're ever watched a non believable show you enjoyed - something like bones comes to mind - this is taking the worse parts of we can rush a story, analysis, evidence, data, blah blah blah but without any of the charm of why it matters.

Interesting idea but a bit of a miss on execution for me and kind of a feeling of  . . .  why did I spend time on this? lol.

review_text_raw: The concept of the operator is super interesting. But unfortunately there's not a lot to explore and investigate here. We're constantly guided by other characters and told the very thing we need to find, one thing after the next. It's like the game never gets past the tutorial, and it never gets to the point where you get to do more advanced research. This simple game mechanic is not super satisfying. It feels more like a short story turned into a game than a real detective game. It's on a very different level compared to other detective games such as Return of the Obra Dinn, The Roottrees are Dead or The Case of the Golden Idol. It's also very short, I finished it in less than 4 hours and there's no replayability. Also be very careful with the saves, there are save points and you'll lose progress if you don't quit at exactly the right times. On the plus side, the interface is quite well done and the voices are nice (though I'm not sure why it makes my computer boiling hot when the graphics are so simple). I liked the bomb defusing part the most, and it's a shame we can't replay that part again.

review_text_raw: Don't get me wrong, it's an interesting story and the final plot twist is one I definitely didn't expect. The UI and the mechanics were interesting, and while it wasn't very hard at least I didn't have to ask for help so it's pretty easy access for people who aren't hardcore into mystery solving. However, I feel like this concept could have gone SO much further- the open ending could have allowed for at least twice as much story and overall I feel like the whole Operator thing should have lasted longer- either been stretched out more in time (because timeline wise this all happens VERY fast) or just... had more to do, more characters to meet? It's supposed to be a full time job and yet we practically only help with a single case a day. In short, I'll repeat what I've seen a lot of other reviews say; this game had a lot of potential. I almost feel like this could be a demo! I bought it on sale, so it's fine, but for a game that has practically only three hours of gameplay I feel like the price (while probably very justified for the developers), isn't really worth it for people with limited funds, especially since there's no real replayability. If you have the money to spare, sure, it's a fun but short game that isn't too hard, but if you want some challenge or you're trying to figure out what to spend your limited allowance on, this probably isn't it.

review_text_raw:
I've been really into narrative puzzle games lately and was excited to give this one a shot. The gameplay and interface are really tight and the story is interesting. However, in terms of a puzzle game it never feels like it ramps up. The story is broken up into such small pieces that there's no real need to sift through different possibilities. Every step towards solution seems pretty obvious. There are fun mechanics introduced and then only used once. You're never really challenged to combine the skills or info you have gathered over the course of the game. In the end it feels like a kind of short visual narrative with a fun interface. If they made another one focused on more difficult scenarios and a wider scope I would probably try it.

Also, nobody had cell phones or digital cameras in 1992/3. Not sure why they chose to set the game in that particular time period, it makes a lot of the technology feel very out of place.

review_text_raw:
I almost never leave reviews, so bear with me.

I was kind of enthralled by the demo: I loved the idea of drawing connections, of looking something up in one database and comparing it to the next database and finding it on a list retrieved earlier.  Then...well, I'm [i]not[/i] going to say is "bait and switch"; I think the demo is a fair representation of the game.  But the game did go in different directions than I'd hoped: for instance, the connection-drawing is in many ways the core of the game, but there was a lot of stuff around it: dialogue choices, minigames  ("oh, look, mastermind"), occasional long cutscenes.

At its core the game is a thriller, which is not really my genre.  (There's literally a "Them", which I think is the same as "The Organization", which is what you get if you ask LLMs to summarize the thriller genre.)  I could have guessed that, probably, but there's so much that seems to pay homage to [i]The X-Files[/i] (the FBI in the 1990s, the typewritten location captions, your boss is literally named Skinner for heaven's sake), and one of the first cases you get is alien-abduction-based.  This ended up being way more "thriller" in tone than X-Files was.

But to be clear: I didn't hate it!  I wish Steam had a scale more subtle than "yes/no", because I want to give it a "qualified yes" or maybe a "no, but if it's your thing, then yes".  There's a lot to like here: the atmosphere (even if you could practically see the words "cue dramatic music" at major plot twists), the interface, even a lot of the writing and plot.  Much of the voice acting is good; I really liked Pendell and Walker; Andrews less so.  (The two coroner reports, even less.)  And the [spoiler]bomb-defusing scene[/spoiler] did a great job with the tone.

Ultimately, I don't [i]regret[/i] playing it.  I also just don't recommend it unless you're looking for a thriller.  In which case, enjoy!

review_text_raw:
This review is unfortunate, because as much as I'd like to recommend the game, there's a few gripes I have with it.

First and foremost, I want to stress, this game is great and has a good hook for its plot. The mechanics it employs are varied and fun, and you do get to feel like an FBI agent working on cases alongside others. The game does a lot to nail the feel and vibe, the UI is also great and intuitive. The game's main issue isn't one singular thing, rather, it's a collection of small, minor nitpicks that ultimately end up souring the entire experience. Without trying to spoil anything, I'm going to try and summarise my complaints. 

First and foremost, the ending left me wanting. If there was an alternate ending you could achieve by using information you've gathered, it'd be one thing, but you don't get to do anything and then it just sort of ends abruptly, teasing a sequel or DLC. This is the very definition of a cliffhanger, and as such, extremely unsatisfying.

This could have been remedied if the game length was longer. But the game's barely clocking in 3 hours, you could probably beat it in 2. And, likely because of said short runtime, the game features a very small cast of characters. This unfortunately results in a somewhat predictable list of potential suspects, lessening any impacts felt from reveals that you likely saw coming.

Perhaps my biggest disappointment with how short the game was, is that the actual mechanics were unique and interesting! The puzzles were good and it introduced so many systems, one time you're analyzing chemical compounds based on formulas, another time you're disarming a bomb while given a huge manual of possibilities. And each of these varied activities happens exactly once. You spend all that time learning, understanding and mastering a skill only for it to literally not be relevant again.

This all could have perhaps been remedied by a sort of "endless mode" that generates cases and solutions, but that does not exist. And likely never will, because the game is far more focused on "immersion" as a central mechanic than gameplay. You spend a good solid 20 minutes of said 3 hours being forced to watch "immersive" unskippable cutscenes that did not need to last as long as they did. I say "immersive", because they use minimalism and only show you blurry, obfuscated imagery, which is kind of neat and saves on budget, but also means you don't even get eye candy.

Ultimately, this feels like a passion project with the wrong focus, which is a shame, because what it does right, it excels at. It's difficult to recommend this when there's games such as Cyber Manhunt 1 & 2 out that cost less and are far, far more superior in terms of value and vision. The devs are talented, and I will keep a close eye on any of their future projects, but if "The Operator 2" doesn't provide something substantially more... substantial, I can't see myself recommending that either.

This all could have perhaps been remedied by a sort of "endless mode" that generates cases and solutions, but that does not exist. And likely never will, because the game is far more focused on "immersion" as a central mechanic than gameplay. You spend a good solid 20 minutes of said 3 hours being forced to watch "immersive" unskippable cutscenes that did not need to last as long as they did. I say "immersive", because they use minimalism and only show you blurry, obfuscated imagery, which is kind of neat and saves on budget, but also means you don't even get eye candy. Ultimately, this feels like a passion project with the wrong focus, which is a shame, because what it does right, it excels at. It's difficult to recommend this when there's games such as Cyber Manhunt 1 & 2 out that cost less and are far, far more superior in terms of value and vision. The devs are talented, and I will keep a close eye on any of their future projects, but if "The Operator 2" doesn't provide something substantially more... substantial, I can't see myself recommending that either.

The ending is a big open wound and comes very abruptly -- just as, in my eyes, the story was just starting to ramp up.
And said ending essentially undoes most of what you did in the game, narratively.
Your ability to interact with the game UI is usually heavily restricted unlike other "hacker" type games that use this presentation style.
In short, everything but the presentation quality is a bit undercooked. Get it on sale, if anything.
